questions.text: If q is false and p ∧ q ↔ r is true, then which one of the following statements is a tautology?
questions.sol_text:
If q is false and p ∧ q ↔ r is true

Since q is false, p ∧ q is false (regardless of the value of p).

For p ∧ q ↔ r to be true, we need p ∧ q and r to have the same truth value.

Since p ∧ q is false, r must be false for the biconditional to be true.

So we have: q is false and r is false.

Now we check each option:

Option (1): p ∧ r
Since r is false, p ∧ r is false. This is not a tautology.

Option (2): (p ∨ r) → (p ∧ r)
From the truth table shown, when p ∧ q ↔ r is true:
- When p = T, q = F, r = F: (p ∨ r) = T, (p ∧ r) = F, so (p ∨ r) → (p ∧ r) = F
- When p = F, q = F, r = F: (p ∨ r) = F, (p ∧ r) = F, so (p ∨ r) → (p ∧ r) = T
This is not a tautology.

Option (3): p ∨ r
Since r is false, p ∨ r = p. This depends on p, so it's not a tautology.

Option (4): (p ∧ r) → (p ∨ r)
From the truth table shown, when p ∧ q ↔ r is true:
- When p = T, q = F, r = F: (p ∧ r) = F, (p ∨ r) = T, so (p ∧ r) → (p ∨ r) = T
- When p = F, q = F, r = F: (p ∧ r) = F, (p ∨ r) = F, so (p ∧ r) → (p ∨ r) = T
This is a tautology.

Therefore, option (4) is the answer.

questions.sol_text:
To determine the nature of the statement (p → (q → p)) → (p → (p ∨ q)), we construct a truth table:

| p | q | q → p | p → (q → p) | p ∨ q | p → (p ∨ q) | (p → (q → p)) → (p → (p ∨ q)) |
|---|---|-------|-------------|-------|-------------|--------------------------------|
| T | T | T     | T           | T     | T           | T                              |
| T | F | T     | T           | T     | T           | T                              |
| F | T | F     | T           | T     | T           | T                              |
| F | F | T     | T           | F     | T           | T                              |

Column 1: p values
Column 2: q values
Column 3: q → p is false only when q is true and p is false
Column 4: p → (q → p) is false only when p is true and (q → p) is false, which never happens here since (q → p) is only false when p is F
Column 5: p ∨ q is true when at least one of p or q is true
Column 6: p → (p ∨ q) is false only when p is true and (p ∨ q) is false, which never happens
Column 7: The final formula (p → (q → p)) → (p → (p ∨ q)) is false only when the antecedent is true and consequent is false

Since the final column contains all T values in every row, the statement is a tautology.

questions.text: Which one of the following is a tautology?
questions.sol_text:
Option 1: P v (P ∧ Q)

Truth table:
P | Q | P ∧ Q | P v (P ∧ Q)
T | T |   T   |     T
T | F |   F   |     T
F | T |   F   |     F
F | F |   F   |     F

Since P v (P ∧ Q) is true whenever P is true (regardless of Q), and false whenever P is false, this is NOT a tautology.

Option 2: Q → (P ∧ (P → Q))
≡ ¬Q v (P ∧ (P → Q))
≡ ¬Q v (P ∧ (¬P v Q))
≡ ¬Q v (P ∧ ¬P) v (P ∧ Q)
≡ ¬Q v f v (P ∧ Q)
≡ ¬Q v (P ∧ Q)
≡ (¬Q v P) ∧ (¬Q v Q)
≡ (¬Q v P) ∧ t
≡ ¬Q v P

This is NOT a tautology.

Option 3: (P ∧ (P → Q)) → Q
≡ (P ∧ (¬P v Q)) → Q
≡ ((P ∧ ¬P) v (P ∧ Q)) → Q
≡ (f v (P ∧ Q)) → Q
≡ (P ∧ Q) → Q
≡ ¬(P ∧ Q) v Q
≡ (¬P v ¬Q) v Q
≡ (¬P) v (¬Q v Q)
≡ (¬P) v t
≡ t

This IS a tautology.

Option 4: P ∧ (P v Q)

Truth table:
P | Q | P v Q | P ∧ (P v Q)
T | T |   T   |     T
T | F |   T   |     T
F | T |   T   |     F
F | F |   F   |     F

This is NOT a tautology.

Therefore, Option 3 is the tautology.

| p | q | ~p | ~q | p v ~q | ~(p v ~q) | p v q | ~(p v ~q) → p v q |
|---|---|----|----|--------|-----------|-------|------------------|
| T | T | F  | F  | T      | F         | T     | T                |
| T | F | F  | T  | T      | F         | T     | T                |
| F | T | T  | F  | F      | T         | T     | T                |
| F | F | T  | T  | T      | F         | F     | T                |

All values in the final column are T, making this a tautology.

For statement (1): p v (~q) → p∧q
When p=T, q=F: p v (~q) = T, p∧q = F, so T → F = F (not a tautology)

For statement (2): ~(p ∧ ~q) → p v q
When p=F, q=F: ~(p ∧ ~q) = T, p v q = F, so T → F = F (not a tautology)

For statement (3): ~(p v ~q) → p∧q
When p=F, q=F: ~(p v ~q) = F, p∧q = F, so F → F = T
When p=F, q=T: ~(p v ~q) = T, p∧q = F, so T → F = F (not a tautology)

Therefore, statement (4) is the tautology.

Statement (C): Since (B) is false, the hypothesis 'both (A) and (B) are true' is false, making the implication vacuously true. Therefore (A) and (C) are true while (B) is false.

The negation of (P AND q) is (~P OR ~q) which equals 'weather is not good or ground is wet'. The negation of the entire statement gives: The match will be played and weather is not good or ground is wet.

However, examining the truth table provided shows (p ∧ q) → (p ∨ q) is a tautology. Therefore * = ∧.

Both P1 and P2 are FALSE
Both P1 and P2 are TRUE
questions.sol_text: Given p → ((~ p) ∨ q) is false. This means p is true and (~ p) ∨ q is false. When p is true: ~ p is false, so F ∨ q = F, which means q is false. Now p = T, q = F. P1: ~ (T → ~ F) = ~ (T → T) = ~ T = FALSE. P2: (T ∧ ~ F) ∧ ((~ T) ∨ F) = (T ∧ T) ∧ (F ∨ F) = T ∧ F = FALSE.

questions.text: The number of choices for Δ ∈ {∧, ∨, ⇒, ↔}, such that (p Δ q) ⇒ ((p ∧ ~q) ∨ (~p Δ q)) is a tautology, is
questions.sol_text: Let x: (p Δ q) ⇒ (p∧~q) ∨ (~p Δ q). Case-I: When Δ is ∨, then (p∨~q) ∨ (~p∨q) is always true, so x is a tautology. Case-II: When Δ is ∧, then (p∧q) ⇒ (p∧~q) ∨ (~p∧q). If p∧q is T, then (p∧~q) ∨ (~p∧q) is F, so x cannot be a tautology. Case-III: When Δ is ⇒, then (p⇒~q) ∨ (~p⇒q) is same as (~p∨~q) ∨ (p∨q), which is always true, so x is a tautology. Case-IV: When Δ is ↔, then (p↔q) ⇒ (p↔~q) ∨ (~p↔q). When p↔q is true, both p↔~q and ~p↔q are false, hence x cannot be a tautology. So x can be ∨ or ⇒, giving 2 choices.

questions.sol_text: Let S: ((~ q) ∧ p) ⇒ ((~ p) ∨ q). Taking negation: ~ S: ~ (((~ q) ∧ p) ⇒ ((~ p) ∨ q)). Using De Morgan's laws and negation of implication: ~ S: (q ∨ (~ p)) ∨ ((~ p) ∨ q). Simplifying: ~ S: (~ p) ∨ q. Which is equivalent to: ~ S: p ⇒ q. Therefore, negation of S is ~ (p ⇒ q).

questions.sol_text: Start with p <=> (q => p). The negation is ~(p <=> (q => p)) which is equivalent to p <=> ~(q => p) which simplifies to p <=> (q ∧ ~p). Converting to disjunctive normal form: (p => (q ∧ ~p)) ∧ ((q ∧ ~p) => p), which further simplifies to (~p ∨ (q ∧ ~p)) ∧ ((~q ∨ p) ∨ p), which reduces to ((~p ∨ q) ∧ ~p) ∧ (~q ∨ p). This simplifies to ~p ∧ (~q ∨ p) which equals (~p ∧ ~q) ∨ (~p ∧ p), which equals (~p ∧ ~q) since (~p ∧ p) is false.

| F | T | T  | F  | F      | T      | T |
| F | F | T  | T  | F      | T      | T |

∴ E is a tautology

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.text: If p, q and r are three propositions, then which of the following combination of truth values of p, q and r makes the logical expression {(p ∨ q) ∧ ((~ p) ∨ r)} → ((~ q) ∨ r) false?
options: p = F, q = T, r = F
p = T, q = F, r = T
p = T, q = T, r = F
p = T, q = F, r = F
questions.sol_text: {(p ∨ q) ∧ ((~ p) ∨ r)} → ((~ q) ∨ r) is false when {(p ∨ q) ∧ ((~ p) ∨ r)} is T and (~ q) ∨ r is F. So, (p ∨ q) = T and (~ p) ∨ r = T and ~ q = F and r = F. So, q = T, r = F, and ~ p = T. ∴ p = F. ∴ p = F, q = T, r = F

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.text: Consider the following statements: P: I have fever, Q: I will not take medicine, R: I will take rest. The statement "If I have fever, then I will take medicine and I will take rest" can be written as which of the following?
questions.sol_text:
The given expression is P → ~ Q ∧ R
≡ (~ P) v (~ Q ∧ R)
≡ ((~ P) v ~ Q) ∧ ((~ P) v R)

Explanation:
1. The statement "If I have fever, then I will take medicine and I will take rest" can be written as: P → (~ Q ∧ R)
2. Using the equivalence P → Q ≡ ~ P v Q, we get:
   P → (~ Q ∧ R) ≡ ~ P v (~ Q ∧ R)
3. Using the distributive law: A v (B ∧ C) ≡ (A v B) ∧ (A v C), we get:
   ~ P v (~ Q ∧ R) ≡ ((~ P) v ~ Q) ∧ ((~ P) v R)

Therefore, the answer is option (3): ((~ P) v ~ Q) ∧ ((~ P) v R)

questions.text:
Among the statements:
(S₁) ((p ∨ q) ⇒ r) ⇔ (p ⇒ r)
(S₂) ((p ∨ q) ⇒ r) ⇔ ((p ⇒ r) ∨ (q ⇒ r))
questions.sol_text:
S₁: ((p ∨ q) ⇒ r) ⇔ (p ⇒ r)
S₂: ((p ∨ q) ⇒ r) ⇔ ((p ⇒ r) ∨ (q ⇒ r))
In S₁: If p = F, q = T, r = F then S₁ is false
In S₂: if p = T, q = F, r = F then S₂ is false
∴ Neither S₁ nor S₂ is a tautology

questions.text: The number of values of r ∈ {p, q, ~p, ~q} for which ((p ∧ q) ⇒ (r ∨ q)) ∧ ((p ∧ r) ⇒ q) is a tautology, is:
questions.sol_text:
((p ∧ q) ⇒ (r ∨ q)) ∧ ((p ∧ r) ⇒ q) ≡ T (given)
= ((~p ∨ ~q) ∨ (r ∨ q)) ∧ (~p ∨ ~r ∨ q)
= ((~p ∨ r) ∨ (~q ∨ q)) ∧ (~p ∨ ~r ∨ q)
= ~p ∨ ~r ∨ q
For above statement to be tautology
r can be ~p or q
∴ Two values of r are possible.

questions.text: (S1) (p ⇒ q) ∨ (p ∧ (~q)) is a tautology (S2) ((~p) ⇒ (~q)) ∧ ((~p) ∨ q) is a contradiction. Then
questions.sol_text:
S1:

| p | q | ~q | p → q | p ∧ (~q) | (p → q) ∨ p ∧ (~q) |
|---|---|----|----|---------|----------|
| T | T | F | T | F | T |
| T | F | T | F | T | T |
| F | T | F | T | F | T |
| F | F | T | T | F | T |

∴ S1 is correct (all values are T, so it is a tautology)

S2:

| p | q | ~q | ~q | ~p → ~q | ~p ∨ q | (S2) |
|---|---|----|----|---------|--------|------|
| T | T | F | F | T | T | T |
| T | F | F | T | T | F | F |
| F | T | T | F | F | T | F |
| F | F | T | T | T | T | T |

∴ S2 is incorrect (not all values are F, so it is not a contradiction)

Option (3) is correct.
